source.title: How Learning Governs Unlearning across the Memorization-Generalization Spectrum
source.authors: Hwiyeong Lee; H. Lim; Ingyu Bang; Hoki Kim; Taeuk Kim

record.file_problem: None apparent; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: It tests a mechanistic explanation of unlearning in a controlled modular-addition setting, measuring whether unlearning damages a shared solution circuit. It does not test the claimed recovery attacks directly.
record.gate_note: The study does not fine-tune an unlearned model to recover knowledge, ablate an activation direction after unlearning, quantize weights, or test prompt-based recovery. Its circuit measurements are relevant to version C's claim that unlearning blocks access rather than damaging the underlying mechanism. Gradient-filtering comparisons alter the unlearning procedure to preserve the circuit; they are not recovery attacks and are not recorded as attack results.
record.test_reason: The study measures retain damage, meaning the drop in performance on kept data, as a function of how much a model relies on memorization versus generalization. It uses modular addition, bucketed modular addition and Hubble LLMs. It never checks whether forgotten knowledge persists or can be recovered: no relearning, direction ablation, quantization or prompting attack. Its Fourier-circuit measurements link circuit damage to retain damage, not to hidden versus deleted forget knowledge, so they fit no version. It cites Eldan & Russinovich, an original source, only as background.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right but incomplete. The authors conclude that retain damage grows with a model's reliance on generalization over memorization. They show this in grokked modular addition (circuit disruption), across a controlled spectrum in bucketed modular addition, and in Hubble LLM verbatim and factual recall. They also argue that retraining without the forget set need not suppress outputs a shared rule produces. They find that redirecting probability to rule-consistent alternatives reduces damage.
record.recipe_differences: Uses RL and GD, among other objectives, to study retain damage and circuit disruption in controlled tasks; it does not reproduce or evaluate the claimed post-unlearning recovery attacks.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported circuit damage is studied in the grokked training phase; the paper also reports that circuit filtering has much larger effects in cleanup and grokked checkpoints than in memorization and circuit-formation checkpoints.

fits_no_version.finding: In the grokked modular-addition model, RL unlearning degrades the shared Fourier circuit: mean FVE falls to 0.186 and restricted loss rises to 2.32. Filtering the key-frequency gradients preserves the circuit and raises retain accuracy from 8.1% to 30.6% (Table 8).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unlearning examples that share a generalizing mechanism with the retain set damages that mechanism, causing retain damage.

fits_no_version.finding: Retain damage falls as the memorization floor rises, in bucketed modular addition (Spearman ρ = -1 in 10 of 12 cells) and in Hubble LLM verbatim and factual recall.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Retain damage from unlearning grows with the model's reliance on generalization over memorization.

record.problems: The direct circuit trajectory values are shown for one forget-set selection seed; the mechanistic experiment is a toy modular-addition setting, not an LLM. Circuit degradation does not by itself establish deletion of all targeted knowledge from the weights.
record.rows_left_out: Not applicable. The gradient-filtering comparisons in Tables 7–8 change the unlearning procedure to preserve the circuit; they are not recovery attacks and do not measure the claimed post-unlearning recovery behavior.

untested.parts: No attacks after unlearning. Retain-damage results bear on utility cost, not on whether unlearning resists recovery.
No relearning or fine-tuning after unlearning.
No activation-direction ablation after unlearning. No analysis of whether forget knowledge is blocked versus deleted.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, multilingual or in-context recovery.
No new method claimed to resist recovery attacks. Gradient filtering and within-bucket relabeling target retain damage, not robustness.

record.verdict_notes: The record's 'tests C / challenges' verdict is not supported. Circuit degradation is used to explain retain damage. Whether the forget answers persist in hidden form is never measured. In modular addition, forget answers come from the same rule as retain answers, so 'deletion' is not a meaningful contrast. The record's row values come from a single seed; the multi-seed means are in Table 8.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test simple attacks after unlearning; its retain-accuracy measurements do not establish the full version.
No post-unlearning fine-tuning or relearning set is used to measure recovery.

Tests the mechanistic alternative that unlearning blocks access rather than damaging a shared circuit, in a toy modular-addition model. Does not ablate a direction after unlearning to test recovery, or test this mechanism in LLMs.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, language variation, or in-context recovery is tested.
Does not evaluate a newer method for resisting the listed recovery attacks.

rows.subject: one-layer ReLU transformer (modular addition, p = 113; grokked checkpoint)
rows.operation_detail: Measured the fraction of logit variance explained by fixed key-frequency Fourier components before and after random-labeling unlearning.

conditions.value: Forget accuracy first falls to chance level (τ = 1/113) or below

rows.measure: FVE (Fraction of Variance Explained) by the key-frequency components
rows.note: The authors interpret the decrease as degradation of the Fourier circuit, not merely loss of access to an intact circuit.
rows.check: FVE of the key-frequency circuit is measured to explain retain damage. It does not show whether forget-set knowledge is hidden or recoverable, so it does not bear on C. The value 0.33 comes from the seed-1 trajectory; Table 8 gives a 5-seed mean of 0.186 ± 0.026 after RL.

rows.subject: one-layer ReLU transformer (modular addition, p = 113; grokked checkpoint)
rows.operation_detail: Measured test cross-entropy using logits reconstructed from the fixed key-frequency Fourier components before and after random-labeling unlearning.

conditions.value: Forget accuracy first falls to chance level (τ = 1/113) or below

rows.measure: Restricted loss of the key-frequency circuit
rows.note: Higher restricted loss means the isolated circuit solves the task less effectively; the authors connect this change to the collapse in retain accuracy.
rows.check: Restricted loss is a measure of circuit integrity tied to retain damage, not a test of recovering unlearned knowledge. The value 2.44 is from seed 1; the 5-seed mean is 2.324 ± 0.183 (Table 8).

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Grokked modular-addition model under RL unlearning
reader_labels.reason: The circuit measurements show substantial degradation rather than an intact circuit that is merely inaccessible (r1, r2); post-unlearning activation ablation and recovery were not tested.
